scope: Bounded exercise dependencies beyond the main complement system. These are explicit teaching/supply proposals, not whole unassigned source passages.

features.description: Behēfe useful takes a dative person to whom the subject is useful. The predicate adjective agrees with its subject, while the recipient noun is dative.
features.prior_status: The exact merchant clause was supplied in Unit8; ordinary productive useful+dative is new.

features.description: Use the nominative-shaped noun in direct address; an accompanying adjective is weak. Thus the morphology of the noun follows number and its own class, while good in O good fellows/workmen uses weak plural. Ēalā is an optional interjection where the original English says O.
features.prior_status: Only an exact merchant vocative was supplied in Unit8.

features.description: The bounded expression Godes ðēowdōm means service of God: God is the object of the service, not necessarily its agent or owner. Use ordinary genitive morphology with this explicitly taught lexical relationship.

Elpes bān means ivory, literally elephant’s bone. The whole expression is supplied for II.10.14: elpes is genitive singular, bān is neuter accusative singular as the thing sold. No rule forming arbitrary material names is inferred.
Āstīgan takes the ship as its direct accusative object in the selected go aboard/board sense. A separate mid+dative phrase names accompanying wares.

For II.12.7 supply libbende gesceafta, living creatures, feminine accusative plural. Libbende follows the documented feminine -e variant of the participial adjective; prior neuter libbendu is a different cell. The phrase is not independently recalled, and no full new libban participle system is assigned.

Productive manig means many as an ordinary attributive adjective agreeing with a plural noun. Its displayed singular cells are recognition reference only; singular many-a, substantival quantity and partitive constructions are outside this lexical scope.

For II.12.13 supply the complete phrase ðrēo hund and fīf and siextig daga, three hundred and sixty-five days. The hundred-unit is counted with neuter ðrēo; fīf and siextig gives five and sixty. Daga is genitive plural in the counted construction. This is a transparent local adaptation of Cook §§78–79, not a claim that Cook prints this exact 365 phrase or that all numerals beyond twelve are now productive.
